name: ゆば料理 東山ゆう豆 (Yuba Ryori Higashiyama Yuzu)

claims.text: Dishes such as the yuba rice topped with egg-yolk soy sauce indicate standard (wheat-based) soy sauce is used in seasoning; no wheat-free soy sauce is advertised.

This is an omnivore kitchen: courses include Kyoto jidori chicken and free-range egg, so plant-based dishes are prepared in a kitchen that also handles animal products. Fish dashi is also likely in soups. Vegan diners should request a fully plant-based arrangement in advance.
The restaurant requests advance notice of allergies and dietary requirements at the time of reservation, suggesting some willingness to accommodate, though no formal vegan/GF protocol is published.

The kitchen centers on house-made, additive-free yuba and a tofu-milk hot pot with Kyoto vegetables — plant-based, soy-forward dishes that form a strong vegetarian-friendly base if animal garnishes (egg, chicken, dashi) are omitted on request.

No information found on dedicated preparation surfaces or equipment for gelato. Pastries and cookies are also served in the same space, raising the possibility of shared utensils or cross-contact. Confirm with staff before ordering if celiac-level safety is required.

Gelato and espresso drinks are the core menu; soy sauce is not a component. However, pastries and cookies on the rotating menu will contain wheat. No dedicated gluten-free labeling has been documented.

Standard gelato is dairy-based (Shinshu milk is the signature ingredient). No dairy-free or vegan gelato options have been confirmed. Fruit sorbets may be dairy-free but this has not been verified in any source.

Owners are internationally experienced (Australian-Japanese) and accustomed to a wide range of customers; communication in basic English is likely possible. No formal allergy protocol has been documented — ask directly about specific flavors and ingredients on the day of your visit.
Gelato is made in-house daily without artificial additives, colorants, or preservatives, using identifiable natural ingredients — a positive baseline for allergen transparency.

name: CHAYADO 百八 善光寺門前 (CHAYADO Momoya Zenkoji Monzen)

claims.text: No information about cross-contamination controls is published. Wheat-containing items (croquet monsieur) are prepared in the same kitchen as gelato and drinks.
No soy sauce appears in the café menu (matcha drinks, gelato, corn soup). Wheat risk from this vector is low, but no allergen sheet has been published to confirm.
Dairy (Kurohime Highland milk) is a core ingredient across gelato and latte menus. No separation or labeling for dairy-free items is documented.

No information about staff allergy training or allergy-handling procedures has been published. The café does not accept reservations (walk-in only), so pre-visit phone enquiry (026-217-2608) is the only available channel to ask about allergen handling before arriving.
The menu is matcha and gelato-focused with minimal processed sauces — simpler ingredient profiles than a full-service restaurant, which reduces (but does not eliminate) hidden allergen risk.
centotto gelato's parent brand emphasises single-origin local produce and minimal-additive gelato-making, which may reduce hidden ingredient complexity.

Tonkatsu is panko-breaded and deep-fried; the fryer is shared and there is no information suggesting a dedicated gluten-free fryer or separate cooking area. Wheat contamination of all fried items should be assumed.
No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce is mentioned. Standard Japanese soy sauce (wheat-containing) is the default at this type of establishment.
All morning sets include egg, dairy (Obuse milk), and likely katsuo/iriko dashi in miso soup. The signature milk udon uses dairy. No plant-based alternatives noted.

No allergy-handling procedures or allergen menu documentation found in any source reviewed. With only 13 seats and full reservation-only operation, direct inquiry by phone before visiting is strongly advisable.

Fully reservation-only format (since May 2021) means small, controlled service — the chef prepares each piece to order and monitors cooking precisely, which allows for meaningful pre-visit allergy conversations.

No dedicated gluten-free kitchen protocols are documented. Soba noodles (which often contain wheat flour in standard Japanese blends) appear across multiple course tiers. Cross-contamination in a shared temple kitchen cannot be excluded.

Standard Japanese soy sauce containing wheat is the default in shojin cooking at this establishment; no mention of tamari or wheat-free soy sauce substitution was found on the official site or in any reviewed source.
The cuisine is 100% plant-based by religious rule — no animal products are used in the kitchen. Vegan cross-contact risk is effectively zero within the shojin framework.

The restaurant requests that all allergies and dietary restrictions be communicated at the time of reservation (事前にお知らせください). Substitutions are available — soba allergies are specifically cited as an example — and additional charges may apply for special accommodations.
The kitchen is entirely free of meat, fish, seafood, eggs, and dairy — a structural advantage for vegan diners and those avoiding animal-derived dashi or broth.
The restaurant explicitly states 「ベジタリアン、ヴィ―ガンの方も安心してお召し上がりいただけます」 (vegetarian and vegan guests can dine with confidence).
No dedicated gluten-free kitchen or protocols mentioned across any reviewed source. Standard French kitchen with house-made bread at every service.
Soy sauce confirmed in at least one vinaigrette preparation (soy and sherry vinegar vinaigrette on seared tuna appetizer), indicating standard wheat-containing shoyu is used.
Dairy (cream, cheese, butter) and animal proteins are core to most course components; no vegan-separated prep line noted.
One source confirms that if dietary restrictions or food allergies are communicated in advance, the kitchen will adjust individual dish contents accordingly.
Vegetable-forward philosophy with over 85% locally sourced Shinshu produce means many course components are plant-based at their core.
Small two-person operation makes customization more feasible than at a large restaurant — direct communication with the kitchen is straightforward.

Buckwheat flour is milled and hand-processed on-site. The restaurant's official site warns of potential cross-contamination from shared preparation surfaces and asks guests with any allergy to notify staff before ordering.

The dipping tsuyu and sauces are made with standard Japanese soy sauce (醤油), which is brewed with wheat. The restaurant's own allergen disclosure lists wheat among the 28 allergens present on the menu. No wheat-free or tamari soy sauce alternative is confirmed.
The primary dashi stock is made from katsuobushi (dried bonito) and Rishiri kombu. All standard dipping sauces contain bonito-based dashi. No vegan broth option is confirmed on the menu.
The official site explicitly states that guests with allergies must inform staff immediately upon arrival, as cross-contamination is possible from on-site buckwheat milling and noodle preparation.
The soba noodles themselves are made from 100% buckwheat (十割) with no wheat binder (つなぎなし), so the noodle strand itself is free of gluten-containing ingredients.

name: 信州善光寺 門前そば処 藤木庵 (Fujikian (Monzen Sobadokoro Fujikian))

claims.text: The restaurant's own posted notice states that because wheat flour is used in many dishes and a noodle-making area with stone milling is inside the shop, even dishes that do not normally contain wheat flour may be contaminated. Not suitable for celiac or wheat-allergic diners.

The mori-tsuyu and kake-tsuyu dipping broths are made with standard soy sauce, which contains wheat. Tamari (wheat-free) soy sauce does not appear to be used based on the published ingredient list (soy sauce, bonito, mackerel, kelp, mirin, sugar, sake).
All dipping broths use two-year-aged dried bonito (本枯節) and mackerel stock. There is no fish-free broth option on the menu.

The restaurant asks that anyone with allergies (soba/buckwheat, wheat, or other allergens) inform staff before ordering. The standard tea served is buckwheat tea, which must also be flagged for buckwheat-allergic guests.

The juwari soba (100% buckwheat, no wheat binder) is available in limited daily quantity and contains no wheat in the noodle itself — though the dipping sauce and kitchen cross-contamination remain concerns.
